chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: Hearing Art Tatum records at Stanley's basement
summary: A maintenance man plays Tatum's Emaline and Moonglow, which seems otherworldly to him compared with Fats Waller.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: In the meantime, he lived in an apartment building, and

the guy who I guess was the maintenance man of the apartment building lived in the basement. He was also an amateur electrician, he fixed things for people. And this fellow, George McIver, used to tell me about this fellow, the maintenance man -- his name was Stanley; I never did know what his last name was. He was telling me about all these records that Stanley had down there. He said, "You ought to hear a record of a guy down there that's he's playing named Art Tatum."

He took me over one time and he played this record for me. The first thing I heard of Art Tatum was a thing I never will forget -- it was called "Emeline". It was "Emeline," there's another one called "Moonglow," and another one called "Beautiful Love." I don't remember exactly what the other one was. I think it was "I Could Do Most Anything For You," but I'm not sure. Anyway, this just floored me. I just didn't believe nobody could make a piano sound like that. As a matter of fact, it was just like listening to somebody from another planet. It didn't even move me to want to play like that. It was just something I figured was not connected with music at all necessarily. It was like if you drive a car well, the idea of driving a race car never occurs to you. And that was just something out of my reach. I just listened and was just mesmerized. I couldn't even imagine myself ever

doing anything like that. I didn't realize really what was going on, because I had heard records of Fats Waller, which I loved very much -- I was trying to play like Fats Waller. But this was just beyond anything I could dream of.
